issues: Both quotes --check FOUND on 2026-09-23. Article 53(1)(c) is quoted from the correct article (Section 2, 'Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models'), and the OJ date is 12.7.2024. The Council register document ST 15698/25 (dated 20 Nov 2025) encloses COM(2025) 837 final of 19.11.2025. The proposal's Article 3 amends the GDPR and inserts Article 88c, and the quoted words are in 88c's second paragraph.

Wording problem 1: calling Art. 53(1)(c) a 'machine-readable opt-out duty' overstates the text. The article obliges GPAI providers to have a copyright policy that identifies and complies with Article 4(3) DSM-directive reservations. 'Machine-readable' comes from the DSM directive, not the AI Act.

Wording problem 2 (substantive): 'an opt-out that is still only a proposal' implies people have no way today to object to their personal data being used for training. That is wrong. GDPR Article 21(1) already gives a right to object to processing based on legitimate interests. The controller can override it only by showing compelling legitimate grounds. What the Omnibus would add is an 'unconditional' version.
Wording problem 3: in the proposed 88c the 'unconditional right to object' is one of a 'such as' list of safeguards, so it is not a free-standing right. The rewording reflects this.

Status check for 'still only a proposal': the European Parliament Legislative Observatory (2025/0360(COD)), fetched 2026-09-23, shows 'Awaiting committee decision'. Its last key event is the committee referral on 19/01/2026. The claim still holds today.

fieldFixes.correction: The one training opt-out the AI Act does recognise is a copyright one. Article 53(1)(c) requires general-purpose model providers to identify and respect rights holders' text-and-data-mining reservations under Article 4(3) of the 2019 copyright directive. It gives individuals no opt-out for their personal data. Personal data remain under the GDPR. There, Article 21 already lets a person object to processing based on legitimate interests, but the controller can override that objection with 'compelling legitimate grounds'. The Commission's November 2025 Digital Omnibus would add an Article 88c that allows AI development on legitimate interests and lists an 'unconditional right to object' among its safeguards. As of September 2026 that is still a proposal awaiting committee decision in the European Parliament.

issues: The Garante quote --check FOUND on 2026-09-23. The page itself is the press release dated 'Rome, 20 December 2024'. The asterisked note about removal was added after the 18 March 2026 judgment. The source date of 2026-03-18 gives the judgment date, not the page date, so it was corrected to 2024-12-20.

Verdict should be FALSE, not MISLEADING. The Court of Rome annulled decision no. 755/2024 in full. ANSA (20 Mar 2026, citing Reuters): 'Il Tribunale di Roma ha annullato una multa di 15 milioni'. So 'definitively fined' is false as of today.

'For training ChatGPT on personal data' is incomplete. The Garante's release and NT+ Diritto list several violations: an unnotified March 2023 breach, no legal basis identified before training, transparency failures, no age verification, and non-compliance with the 2023 communication order. Training was one of these.

The judgment's reasoning, which the record says was not reviewed, is now established. NT+ Diritto (Il Sole 24 Ore, 3 Jun 2026) reports that the court upheld OpenAI's first ground only: from 15 Feb 2024, OpenAI Ireland Ltd.'s sole EU establishment moved competence to the Irish lead authority under the GDPR one-stop-shop. The court held that the merits 'resta non esaminato'. The fine had been suspended by order of 21 March 2025. The Garante could still appeal to the Court of Cassation.
The Garante says the decision was 'temporarily' removed. The correction dropped that word, and it has been restored.

fieldFixes.correction: The Garante did impose EUR 15 million, in decision no. 755 of 2 November 2024 (announced 20 December 2024). The fine covered several GDPR breaches, not just training: training ChatGPT on users' data without a prior legal basis, transparency failures, no age verification, and an unreported March 2023 data breach. The Court of Rome suspended the fine in March 2025. It then annulled the decision in judgment no. 4153/2026, published 18 March 2026, and the Garante has temporarily removed the decision from its website. The annulment was on a preliminary point, not the merits: once OpenAI had set up its sole EU establishment in Ireland (recognised 15 February 2024), competence passed to the Irish lead authority under the GDPR's one-stop-shop. Whether the training was lawful was left unexamined, and the Garante could still appeal to the Court of Cassation.

issues: Both quotes --check FOUND on 2026-09-23 (IEEE 7012 abstract; MyTerms FAQ Q15). The IEEE page details match the correction: the first party points to agreements and the second party 'shall accept one'; the agreement is 'signed electronically by both parties or their agents'; and 'a matching record shall be kept by both sides in a form that can be retrieved, audited, or disputed'.

Problem: 'DNT and GPC are one-way signals responding to choices framed by sites' is inaccurate. It borrows the MyTerms FAQ's framing. DNT and GPC are user-initiated browser signals and are not framed by sites. GPC is a single header value ('Sec-GPC: 1') conveying 'a person's request to websites and services to not sell or share their personal information', and its force comes from laws such as the CCPA (W3C GPC Working Draft, 17 Sep 2026). The accurate contrast is request versus agreement, not reactive versus proactive. The correction was rewritten.

The claim that the transport 'may resemble a browser header' is supported by the MyTerms FAQ itself: 'including browser headers (on the model of Do Not Track and Global Privacy Conrol)' (typo verbatim, FOUND). This was added as a source.

fieldFixes.correction: DNT and GPC are one-way preference signals. The browser sends a single header value asking sites not to track, or not to sell or share personal data. Whether that binds anyone depends on the site or on a law such as California's, and no agreement is formed. IEEE 7012 makes the individual the first party who proffers standard-form contractual terms. The site accepts one, both sides (or their agents) sign, and each keeps a matching record that can be audited or disputed. MyTerms may travel in a browser header 'on the model of' DNT and GPC, but its legal form is different: an agreement with records. (The characterisation of MyTerms as an enforceable contract is the project's own and is untested in court.)

issues: All three evidence quotes --check FOUND on 2026-09-23: Pew (2023-10-18), the Linux Foundation AAIF release (dateline 'SAN FRANCISCO, Dec. 9, 2025') and the ICO innovation-opportunities page. The ICO subpage's DC.Date meta reads 12 Dec 2025. The report was published on 8 Jan 2026, per the landing page and a prior verifier, so the date was kept.

'MCP ... connected agents to more than 10,000 published servers within a year' is off by a few weeks. MCP was open-sourced on 25 Nov 2024 (Anthropic). The 10,000 figure is from the 9 Dec 2025 LF release, about 12.5 months later. This was reworded to 'little more than a year after its November 2024 launch'. The LF figure also counts published servers, not connections.

'agent-to-agent and payment protocols launched with 50 and 60-plus corporate partners' was unsourced in the record. Checked: Google's A2A launch (9 Apr 2025) cites 'more than 50 technology partners', with service providers such as Accenture and Deloitte listed separately. Google's AP2 launch (16 Sep 2025) says 'more than 60 organizations'. Every AP2 partner it names is a company, but the source's own word is 'organizations'. The explanation was reworded to 'more than 50 and more than 60 partner organisations', and both launch posts were added as evidence.
The Pew figure concerns U.S. adults ('Americans'), and 'frequently' in Pew's wording covers always/almost always/often. The paraphrase 'frequently click agree unread' is faithful.

The evidence array is replaced wholesale via fieldFixes.evidence, not via sourceFixes/addSources, because tools/apply-verdicts.py only edits 'sources'/'source' and would otherwise create a stray empty 'sources' list on this record.

fieldFixes.explanation: Even before agents, most people did not read privacy terms: 56% of Americans frequently click 'agree' without reading, and two in five UK adults never read cookie policies. One protocol alone, MCP, had more than 10,000 published servers for agents to connect to little more than a year after its November 2024 launch. The agent-to-agent (A2A) and agent-payments (AP2) protocols launched with more than 50 and more than 60 partner organisations respectively. Delegation multiplies the number of counterparties while removing the human reader entirely.
